title: Constrained Optimization and Duality
description: Lagrange multipliers, the KKT conditions, Lagrangian duality and their use for support vector machines, PCA, maximum entropy and regularization.
overview: Many problems ask for the best point subject to restrictions: probabilities must be non-negative and sum to one, a weight vector must have norm at most one, a classifier must separate the data with a margin. The method of Lagrange multipliers turns a constrained problem into an unconstrained one by pricing the constraints. The prices, the multipliers, are not just a trick: they measure how much the optimum would improve if a constraint were relaxed.

The resulting Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions are the first-order optimality conditions for constrained problems. Duality builds on the same Lagrangian a second problem, whose solution bounds and often equals the original one. Duality gave the support vector machine its kernel form, and it explains several results of the Machine Learning book.
objectives: Solve equality-constrained problems with Lagrange multipliers and interpret the multiplier geometrically.
Write the Lagrangian and the KKT conditions for a problem with inequality constraints, and solve small examples.
Form the dual function and dual problem, and state weak and strong duality.
Derive the dual of the hard-margin support vector machine.
Use constrained optimization to derive PCA, maximum entropy distributions and the equivalence of constrained and penalized regularization.

sections.title: Equality constraints and Lagrange multipliers
body: Suppose you want to reach the lowest point of a hillside, but you must stay on a particular hiking trail. On the trail, you can walk until the ground along the trail stops going down. At that spot the trail is tangent to a contour line of the hill: moving along the trail no longer changes your height, and the only direction of steeper descent points off the trail, which you are not allowed to take. Lagrange multipliers turn this picture into an equation. Minimize f(x) subject to h(x) = 0. At a constrained minimum, the gradient of f must be perpendicular to the constraint surface (otherwise we could slide along the surface and lower f), so it is parallel to the gradient of h, which is also perpendicular to the surface:

body.caption: Minimize x² + y² subject to x + 2y = 5. The constraint line (blue) touches the lowest reachable level curve at (1, 2), where the two curves are tangent and their gradients are parallel.

body: The same condition is obtained by forming the **Lagrangian** L(x, ν) = f(x) − ν h(x) and setting all its partial derivatives, with respect to x and the multiplier ν, to zero. The derivative with respect to ν returns the constraint h(x) = 0, and the derivatives with respect to x give the parallel-gradient condition. For several constraints h_j use one multiplier each.

example.title: Closest point on a line
example.problem: Minimize x² + y² subject to x + 2y = 5.
example.solution: ∇f = (2x, 2y) = ν(1, 2), so x = ν/2 and y = ν. The constraint gives ν/2 + 2ν = 5, so ν = 2, x = 1, y = 2, and f = 5. The multiplier ν = 2 is the rate at which the optimal value would grow with the constraint level: if the constraint were x + 2y = 5 + δ the optimum would be (5 + δ)²/5, whose derivative at δ = 0 is 2 ✓.

example.title: Maximize a product
example.problem: Maximize xy subject to x + y = 10.
example.solution: L = xy − ν(x + y − 10). ∂/∂x: y = ν. ∂/∂y: x = ν. So x = y = 5 and the maximum is 25.

list: **PCA**: maximize uᵀΣu subject to uᵀu = 1. The Lagrangian uᵀΣu − λ(uᵀu − 1) has gradient 2Σu − 2λu = 0, i.e. Σu = λu: the optimal direction is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix, and the objective equals λ (see PCA and Dimensionality Reduction).

**Maximum entropy**: maximize −Σp_i ln p_i subject to Σp_i = 1. The Lagrangian's derivative is −ln p_i − 1 − ν = 0, which gives the same p_i for every i: the uniform distribution, p_i = 1/n, is the maximum entropy distribution on n outcomes. Adding a constraint on the mean E[x] gives p_i ∝ e^{−βx_i}, the exponential family (the Gibbs or softmax form).

check.q: At a constrained optimum with one equality constraint h(x) = 0, the gradient of f is
check.a: parallel to the gradient of h
wrong: perpendicular to the gradient of h

sections.title: Inequality constraints and the KKT conditions
body: Now let the trail become a region you must stay within, such as a fenced field. If the lowest point of the hill is inside the field, the fence does not matter. If it is outside, the best you can do is stand against the fence, and the fence is then actively holding you back. The KKT conditions say exactly this: a constraint that is not touched has no effect (its multiplier is zero), and a constraint that you are pressed against pushes back with a force equal to its multiplier. Consider the general problem

eq: subject to g_i(x) ≤ 0 (i = 1, …, m),  h_j(x) = 0 (j = 1, …, p)

body: with the Lagrangian L(x, λ, ν) = f(x) + Σλ_ig_i(x) + Σν_jh_j(x), where the multipliers of the inequality constraints satisfy λ_i ≥ 0. The **Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions** for a point x* with multipliers (λ*, ν*) are:

Complementary slackness says that each constraint is either **active** (g_i = 0, the optimum sits on its boundary, and its multiplier may be positive) or inactive (g_i < 0, and then its multiplier is zero, as if the constraint were absent). The KKT conditions are necessary for optimality under mild regularity assumptions, and, for a **convex** problem, they are also **sufficient**: any point satisfying them is a global minimum.

example.title: An active constraint
solution: The unconstrained minimum (2, 2) violates the constraint (x + y = 4 > 2), so we expect the constraint to be active: x + y = 2.
Stationarity with g = x + y − 2: (2(x − 2), 2(y − 2)) + λ(1, 1) = 0, giving x = y = 2 − λ/2. With x + y = 2, we get λ = 2, x = y = 1.
Check: λ = 2 ≥ 0 ✓, g = 0 ✓. The optimum (1, 1) is the projection of (2, 2) onto the half-plane, with value 2.

example.title: An inactive constraint
example.solution: The unconstrained minimum (0.5, 0.5) has x + y = 1 < 2, so it is feasible and the constraint is inactive: λ = 0 by complementary slackness, and the solution is (0.5, 0.5). The constraint plays no role.

example.title: A one-dimensional problem
example.problem: Minimize x² subject to x ≥ 1, i.e. g(x) = 1 − x ≤ 0.
example.solution: Stationarity: 2x − λ = 0. If λ = 0 then x = 0, which is infeasible, so g is active: x = 1 and λ = 2 > 0 ✓. All four conditions hold, and since the problem is convex, x* = 1 is the global minimum.

body: Let p*(b) be the optimal value when the constraint is relaxed to g(x) ≤ b. Then dp*/db = −λ* (at b = 0): the multiplier is the marginal gain, in objective units, from loosening the constraint by one unit (the shadow price). In the one-dimensional example above, p*(b) = b² for b ≥ 0 so that relaxing the constraint to x ≥ 1 − ε would change the value by about −2ε, matching λ = 2.

check.q: Complementary slackness requires that for each inequality constraint
check.a: either the multiplier is zero or the constraint holds with equality
wrong: the multiplier equals the constraint value

sections.title: Lagrangian duality
body: Call the original problem the **primal** problem with optimal value p*. The **dual function** is the minimum of the Lagrangian over x:

body.eq: g(λ, ν) = inf_x L(x, λ, ν),    λ ≥ 0

body: For any feasible x and any λ ≥ 0, L(x, λ, ν) ≤ f(x) (the added terms Σλ_ig_i are ≤ 0 and Σν_jh_j = 0), so g(λ, ν) ≤ p*: the dual function is a lower bound on the primal optimum. This is **weak duality**. The **dual problem** looks for the best bound:

body.eq: d* = max_{λ ≥ 0, ν} g(λ, ν) ≤ p*

body: The dual function is always concave (it is an infimum of functions affine in (λ, ν)), so the dual problem is a concave maximization, i.e. convex, even if the primal is not. The difference p* − d* ≥ 0 is the **duality gap**. For convex problems satisfying a mild condition (**Slater's condition**: there is a strictly feasible point), **strong duality** holds: d* = p*, and the KKT conditions characterize the optimum of both.

example.title: The dual of a simple problem
example.problem: Form and solve the dual of: minimize x² subject to x ≥ 1.
example.solution: L(x, λ) = x² + λ(1 − x). Minimizing over x: 2x − λ = 0 gives x = λ/2, so g(λ) = λ²/4 + λ − λ²/2 = λ − λ²/4. Maximize over λ ≥ 0: g′ = 1 − λ/2 = 0 gives λ = 2 and g(2) = 2 − 1 = 1. This equals the primal optimum p* = 1: there is no gap, and the optimal dual variable is the multiplier found before.

list: The dual problem has one variable per constraint, so it can be much smaller than the primal when there are few constraints and many variables, or the reverse.
From a dual solution, the primal solution is recovered by minimizing the Lagrangian at the optimal multipliers.
Dual variables give **certificates**: any feasible (λ, ν) bounds p* from below, so an algorithm can stop when the primal value and the dual bound are close.
Duality underlies many algorithms: SVM solvers (SMO), ADMM, and the interior-point methods for convex programs.

check.q: Weak duality says that the dual optimal value d* is
check.a: at most the primal optimal value p*

sections.title: Application: the support vector machine dual
body: The hard-margin support vector machine (see Support Vector Machines and Kernels) is the convex problem

eq: subject to 1 − y_i(wᵀx_i + b) ≤ 0,  i = 1, …, m

body: Its Lagrangian, with multipliers α_i ≥ 0, is L = ½‖w‖² − Σα_i[y_i(wᵀx_i + b) − 1]. Minimizing over the primal variables (w, b):
Substituting back gives the dual function, which depends on the data only through inner products:

body.eq: g(α) = Σα_i − ½ ΣΣ α_iα_jy_iy_j x_iᵀx_j,    α ≥ 0, Σα_iy_i = 0

body: The problem is convex with affine constraints, so strong duality holds, and the KKT conditions give complementary slackness: α_i[y_i(wᵀx_i + b) − 1] = 0. A point either has α_i = 0 or lies exactly on the margin; the latter are the **support vectors**. Replacing x_iᵀx_j by a kernel K(x_i, x_j) is the kernel trick.

example.title: Why only support vectors matter
example.problem: In the two-point example of the SVM chapter, x₁ = 0 (y = −1) and x₂ = 2 (y = +1), the optimal dual variables are α₁ = α₂ = 1/2. Which constraints are active, and what is the margin?
example.solution: Both α_i > 0, so both constraints are active: the points lie on the margin. w = ½(−1)(0) + ½(+1)(2) = 1, and b = −1 from the active constraint at x₂. The dual value is Σα − ½(α²)(x₂²) = 1 − ½(¼)(4) = 0.5 = ½‖w‖², so there is no duality gap.

sections.title: Constraints, penalties and algorithms
body: Ridge regression can be posed as a constrained problem, minimize ‖Xθ − y‖² subject to ‖θ‖² ≤ t, or as the penalized problem minimize ‖Xθ − y‖² + λ‖θ‖². The Lagrangian of the first is the objective of the second, with the multiplier λ. For every t > 0 there is a λ ≥ 0 with the same solution (and vice versa), and λ is the price of the norm budget: by complementary slackness, λ = 0 if the unconstrained least squares solution already satisfies the constraint, and otherwise the constraint is active. The same holds for the lasso, with ‖θ‖₁ ≤ t. This is the equivalence between the 'ball' and the 'penalty' pictures in the Regularization chapter.

example.title: Ridge as a constrained problem
example.problem: Minimize (θ − 3)² subject to θ² ≤ 4. Find θ and the multiplier.
example.solution: The unconstrained minimum 3 violates |θ| ≤ 2, so the constraint is active: θ = 2. Stationarity: 2(θ − 3) + λ(2θ) = 0 gives −2 + 4λ = 0, so λ = 0.5. The equivalent penalized problem (θ − 3)² + 0.5θ² has minimizer θ = 3/(1 + 0.5) = 2 ✓.

list: **Projected gradient descent**: take a gradient step, then project back onto the feasible set C: x ← Π_C(x − α∇f(x)). Works when the projection is easy, for example onto a ball (rescale), a box (clip), or the probability simplex (a sort-and-threshold algorithm).

**Penalty and barrier methods**: replace the constraints by a penalty for violating them, or, in an **interior-point method**, by a logarithmic barrier −(1/t)Σln(−g_i(x)) that keeps the iterates strictly inside the feasible set, with t increased gradually. Interior-point methods solve LPs and QPs in tens of Newton iterations.

**ADMM** (alternating direction method of multipliers) splits a problem into pieces that are solved separately and coordinated through dual variables. It is popular for distributed and structured problems.
**Frank–Wolfe** minimizes a linear approximation over the feasible set, which is cheap for polytopes and nuclear-norm balls.

In training with the softmax or a normalized weight, constraints are enforced by parameterization (softmax ensures non-negative weights that sum to one) so that unconstrained optimization can be used.

check.q: In projected gradient descent, after each gradient step the iterate is
check.a: projected back onto the feasible set
wrong: moved along the constraint normal only

quiz.q: Minimize x² + y² subject to 3x + 4y = 25. What is the minimum value?
quiz.why: ∇f = (2x, 2y) = ν(3, 4) puts the optimum on the line through (3, 4), and 3x + 4y = 25 gives (x, y) = (3, 4) with f = 25. The value 5 is the distance, not its square.

quiz.q: For minimize x² + y² subject to 3x + 4y = c, the optimal value is c²/25. If c rises from 25 to 26, the optimal value rises by about
quiz.why: The derivative of c²/25 at c = 25 is 2c/25 = 2, which equals the multiplier ν. The exact change is 676/25 − 25 = 2.04.

quiz.q: Why must ∇f be parallel to ∇h at a minimum of f subject to h(x) = 0?
quiz.a: Otherwise a step along the constraint surface would still lower f
wrong: Because f is constant everywhere on the constraint surface
Because the multiplier is always positive
Because ∇h is zero at the minimum
quiz.why: If ∇f had a component along the surface, sliding that way would decrease f while staying feasible. Only the component perpendicular to the surface, along ∇h, can remain.

quiz.q: Σ = [[3, 1], [1, 3]]. What is the maximum of uᵀΣu over unit vectors u?
quiz.why: The Lagrangian condition Σu = λu makes the objective equal to an eigenvalue. The eigenvalues are 4 and 2, so the maximum is 4; the value 6 is the trace.

quiz.q: Maximizing entropy over a distribution on {x₁, …, x_n} with the normalization constraint and a fixed mean E[x] gives probabilities of the form
quiz.why: Adding a linear constraint on the mean adds a term βx_i to the stationarity condition, giving an exponential (Gibbs) form. The uniform distribution is optimal only with normalization alone.

quiz.q: A candidate point satisfies stationarity, primal feasibility and complementary slackness, but one inequality multiplier is λ = −1. What can be said?
quiz.a: It is not a KKT point, because dual feasibility λ ≥ 0 fails
wrong: It is a KKT point, since the other three conditions hold
It is a global minimum, since the problem is convex
It is a KKT point only if the constraint is inactive
quiz.why: All four conditions must hold. A negative multiplier would mean the constraint pulls the point inward, so the point could be improved by moving off the boundary.

quiz.q: Minimize (x − 3)² + (y − 1)² subject to x + y ≤ 2. What are the solution and the multiplier?
quiz.why: The unconstrained minimum (3, 1) has x + y = 4 > 2, so the constraint is active. Stationarity gives x = 3 − λ/2 and y = 1 − λ/2, and x + y = 2 gives λ = 2, so (x, y) = (2, 0).

quiz.q: Minimize x² + y² subject to x + y ≤ 4. What are the solution and the multiplier?
quiz.why: The unconstrained minimum (0, 0) already satisfies x + y ≤ 4, so the constraint is inactive and complementary slackness forces λ = 0. Treating it as active would move to the boundary needlessly.

quiz.q: Minimize x² subject to x ≥ 1, where the multiplier is 2. If the constraint is relaxed to x ≥ 0.9, the optimal value falls by about
quiz.why: The multiplier is the shadow price: a relaxation of 0.1 changes the value by about 2 × 0.1 = 0.2. The exact change is 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.

quiz.q: In a minimization problem, a dual feasible point has dual function value g(λ, ν) = 3.2. What follows about the primal optimum p*?
quiz.why: Weak duality says every dual value is a lower bound on p*. Equality needs strong duality and an optimal dual point.

quiz.q: For minimize x² subject to x ≥ 3, the dual function is g(λ) = 3λ − λ²/4 for λ ≥ 0. What is the optimal dual value d*?
quiz.why: g′(λ) = 3 − λ/2 = 0 gives λ = 6, and g(6) = 18 − 9 = 9. This equals the primal optimum 3² = 9, so there is no duality gap; λ = 6 is the optimal dual variable, not the value.

quiz.q: What can be said about the dual function g(λ, ν) = inf_x L(x, λ, ν) of any problem?
quiz.a: It is concave, even when the primal problem is not convex
wrong: It is convex whenever the primal is convex
It is convex, because it is a minimum over x
quiz.why: For each x the Lagrangian is affine in (λ, ν), and a pointwise infimum of affine functions is concave. It is not linear in general.

quiz.q: Which condition guarantees strong duality, d* = p*?
quiz.a: A convex problem with a strictly feasible point (Slater's condition)
wrong: Any problem with at least one inequality constraint
Any problem whose objective is differentiable
Any problem whose dual function is concave
quiz.why: Convexity together with a strictly feasible point removes the duality gap. The dual function is concave for every problem, so that cannot be the deciding property.

quiz.q: In a hard-margin SVM the points x₁ = 1 (y = −1) and x₂ = 3 (y = +1) have α₁ = α₂ = 0.5. What are w and b?
quiz.why: w = Σα_iy_ix_i = −0.5(1) + 0.5(3) = 1. The active constraint at x₂ gives y(wx + b) = 3 + b = 1, so b = −2, placing the boundary at x = 2, midway between the points.

quiz.q: A training point in a hard-margin SVM satisfies y(wᵀx + b) = 1.8. What is its dual variable α?
quiz.a: 0, so it is not a support vector
wrong: positive, since every training point contributes to w
undetermined, since the constraint is satisfied
quiz.why: Complementary slackness α[y(wᵀx + b) − 1] = 0 forces α = 0 when the constraint is strictly satisfied. Only points exactly on the margin can have α > 0 and appear in w.

quiz.q: Minimize (θ − 6)² subject to θ² ≤ 9. Which penalty λ in (θ − 6)² + λθ² gives the same solution?
quiz.why: The constraint is active at θ = 3, and stationarity 2(θ − 6) + 2λθ = 0 gives −6 + 6λ = 0, so λ = 1. Check: the penalized minimizer is 6/(1 + λ) = 3.

quiz.q: In ridge regression written as minimize ‖Xθ − y‖² subject to ‖θ‖² ≤ t, the least squares solution already has ‖θ‖² = 2 and t = 5. What is the multiplier λ?
wrong: Positive but unknown without more information
Negative, since the constraint has slack
quiz.why: The constraint is inactive, so complementary slackness gives λ = 0 and the constrained and unconstrained solutions coincide. A multiplier of an inequality constraint is never negative.

quiz.q: A gradient step lands at (1.4, −0.3, 0.6), and the feasible set is the box [0, 1]³. What is the projection used by projected gradient descent?
wrong: (1.4, −0.3, 0.6), since a projection leaves feasible directions alone
quiz.why: Projection onto a box clips each coordinate to [0, 1]: 1.4 becomes 1, −0.3 becomes 0, and 0.6 is unchanged. Rescaling is the projection onto a ball, not a box.

summary: With an equality constraint, ∇f = ν∇h at the optimum: the gradients are parallel. Solve with the Lagrangian L = f − νh and set all derivatives to zero. PCA (Σu = λu) and the maximum entropy (uniform, or Gibbs) distribution are examples.

With inequality constraints g_i ≤ 0, the KKT conditions are stationarity, primal feasibility, λ ≥ 0 and complementary slackness (λ_ig_i = 0). They are sufficient for convex problems. A multiplier is the shadow price of its constraint.
The dual function g(λ, ν) = inf_x L is concave and bounds the primal optimum from below (weak duality). Under Slater's condition for convex problems, d* = p* (strong duality).
The SVM dual has only inner products of data points, the support vectors are those with α_i > 0, and the kernel trick follows.
Constrained and penalized regularization are equivalent, with λ as the multiplier. Projected gradient, interior-point and ADMM methods solve constrained problems.

problems.q: Minimize x² + y² + z² subject to x + y + z = 3.
problems.solution: 2x = 2y = 2z = ν, so x = y = z and 3x = 3 gives x = y = z = 1. The minimum is 3, with ν = 2.

problems.q: Maximize x + y subject to x² + y² = 2.
problems.solution: ∇(x + y) = (1, 1) = ν(2x, 2y), so x = y = 1/(2ν). Then 2x² = 2 gives x = ±1. The maximum is at (1, 1) with value 2 (and the minimum at (−1, −1), value −2).

problems.q: Solve: minimize x² + y² subject to x + y ≥ 4. Give the multiplier.
problems.solution: Write g = 4 − x − y ≤ 0. Stationarity: (2x − λ, 2y − λ) = 0, so x = y = λ/2. The constraint is active (the unconstrained minimum 0 is infeasible): x + y = 4 gives x = y = 2 and λ = 4 > 0. The minimum value is 8.

problems.q: Form the dual of: minimize ½x² subject to x ≥ 2 and show strong duality.
problems.solution: L = ½x² + λ(2 − x), minimized at x = λ, giving g(λ) = ½λ² + 2λ − λ² = 2λ − ½λ². Maximizing: λ = 2, g = 4 − 2 = 2. The primal optimum is x = 2 with ½x² = 2. So d* = p* = 2.

problems.q: Show that the maximum entropy distribution on {1, 2, 3} with no constraints other than normalization is uniform, and compute its entropy.
problems.solution: The Lagrangian −Σp ln p − ν(Σp − 1) gives −ln p_i − 1 − ν = 0, so all p_i are equal, p_i = 1/3. The entropy is ln 3 = 1.0986 nats (1.585 bits).
